misconceptions.description: Equating adapting for variability with giving advanced students more work and struggling students less of the same work
misconceptions.trigger: teacher's adaptation only changes quantity, leaving the cognitive demand and access identical
misconceptions.feedback: Adapt the path to the objective, not the page count. More or fewer items rarely changes who can reach the goal.

misconceptions.description: Treating an accommodation as a reason to lower the learning goal rather than to change the route to the same goal
misconceptions.trigger: teacher swaps the grade-level objective for an easier one when providing support
misconceptions.feedback: An accommodation changes access, not the target. Keep the objective; change the scaffold, format, or time.

misconceptions.description: Adapting based on a category label such as ELL or IEP rather than the specific barrier the student faces in this task
misconceptions.trigger: teacher applies a generic accommodation tied to a label without naming the task-specific barrier
misconceptions.feedback: Name the barrier this task creates for this student, then adapt to that barrier. Labels are not lesson plans.

misconceptions.description: Assuming an AI text simplification preserved the cognitive demand when it actually stripped out the complexity the objective asked students to analyze.
misconceptions.trigger: teacher assigns an AI-simplified source without comparing its demand to the original
misconceptions.feedback: Compare the adapted task's demand to the original before trusting it: easier reading is not the same thinking. If the objective asks students to analyze competing causes and the simplification removed all but one cause, the goal was quietly lowered in disguise.
